title: Managing Distributed Workflows
subtitle: Choose coordination for the workflow you actually have
summary: Distributed workflows combine services to perform domain work, so their design is governed by communication, consistency, and coordination. Orchestration gives one workflow specific mediator responsibility for state, alternate paths, retries, and errors. Choreography distributes those responsibilities across participating services and can reduce a central bottleneck, but error paths add communication links and domain complexity. Neither style removes semantic coupling: the business workflow already requires its steps. Implementation can only add to that coupling. Choreography also needs a deliberate state strategy, such as a front controller, rebuilding state from services, or stamping state into messages. The chapter’s practical lesson is to model normal and failure paths together, then choose the smallest coordination structure that fits the workflow’s complexity, scale, and status needs.

concepts.title: Orchestration
concepts.body: An orchestrator manages one workflow’s state, calls, optional behavior, errors, notifications, and retries. It should be specific to that workflow rather than a global enterprise bus. This central owner makes complex alternate paths visible and queryable, while adding a communication bottleneck, a possible failure point, and coupling to every participating service.
concepts.example: An order orchestrator records the order, verifies payment synchronously, asks fulfillment asynchronously, and emails the customer. If fulfillment reports a backorder, it refunds payment and updates order status.

concepts.title: Choreography
concepts.body: In choreography, each service performs its local step and emits a message that triggers the next participant. The happy path has fewer coordination components, but boundary paths force services to know how to notify, compensate, or update one another. As the workflow grows, those extra links can become a distributed mediator in everything but name.
concepts.example: Order placement emits a payment message; payment emits fulfillment; fulfillment emits email. A backorder then requires compensating messages to payment, email, and order placement.

concepts.title: Semantic coupling
concepts.body: A domain workflow has inherent semantic coupling: its required steps and dependencies come from the business problem. An architect cannot eliminate that coupling through topology. Technical layers or accidental service links can increase it, so organizing implementation around domain workflows usually keeps the solution closer to the problem’s actual complexity.
concepts.example: Ticket assignment must match skills, schedules, and locations. A domain partition keeps that workflow together; technical layers smear it across persistence, rules, and presentation and add coordination work.

concepts.title: Workflow state
concepts.body: Choreography needs an explicit answer to where transient state lives. A front controller makes status easy to query but adds a pseudo-mediator and communication chatter. Stateless choreography reconstructs a snapshot by querying every service, improving decoupling at a cost in latency. Stamp coupling carries state in messages, reducing queries while enlarging contracts and still lacking a single status owner.
concepts.example: For an order, a front controller stores workflow progress; a stateless design queries order, payment, and fulfillment; a stamped message carries completed steps to the next service.

misconceptions.claim: Choreography is always the more decoupled and therefore better choice.
misconceptions.correction: It removes a mediator, but complex error paths add service links and workflow knowledge. Compare the full happy path, failure paths, state queries, and scale needs.

misconceptions.claim: A mediator removes the workflow’s coupling.
misconceptions.correction: The domain steps still have semantic coupling. Orchestration centralizes implementation and can make it easier to reason about, while also creating a coupling point and bottleneck.

scenario.title: Coordinate ticket assignment
scenario.context: A support platform must accept a ticket, match skills, check schedules, assign an engineer, and report status. Matching rules change often, failures need clear recovery, and operators want to query progress. Traffic is moderate today but may grow. Choose a coordination style while accounting for error paths and the cost of putting workflow knowledge in domain services.

options.label: Workflow orchestrator
options.benefit: One component owns progress, retries, alternate paths, and a status view.
options.cost: The mediator adds coupling, a throughput chokepoint, and a workflow failure concern.
options.consequence: A failed schedule lookup is retried and then routed to an explicit exception state. Operators query one workflow record, while the team monitors mediator load and availability.

options.label: Service choreography
options.benefit: Services can process the normal chain without a central coordinator and avoid one workflow bottleneck.
options.cost: Each participant must understand failure notifications, state reconstruction, and compensation.
options.consequence: Skill matching emits a schedule request and later events complete assignment. A partial failure requires several services to publish corrective events, increasing operational investigation work.

scenario.debrief: The number of alternate paths and the need for an authoritative status view favor orchestration here. A simpler, high-throughput chain with rare errors could justify choreography. The domain semantics remain the same in either design.

quiz.question: What distinguishes orchestration from choreography?
options: An orchestrator owns coordination for one workflow
Choreography requires a global enterprise bus
Orchestration makes every service share one database
quiz.explanation: Orchestration introduces a workflow-specific mediator. Choreography distributes triggering and coordination among services.

quiz.question: Why can choreography become harder as error cases increase?
options: Each service must add links and logic for alternate paths and compensation
Eventual consistency makes all errors impossible
quiz.explanation: Error paths add communication and workflow knowledge to domain services, even when the happy path is simple.

quiz.question: Which state choice provides a single easy status query but adds chatter?
quiz.explanation: A front controller owns workflow state, simplifying queries while requiring services to communicate with that owner.

exercise.title: Map both workflow paths
exercise.prompt: Draw the happy path and two failure paths for a multi-service workflow. Compare orchestration and choreography, then record who owns transient state and how an operator queries it.

steps.text: A client starts a domain workflow with its required semantic steps.
Choose a mediator or distributed event chain and define failure routes.
Services perform local work and report success, failure, or compensation.
Persist or reconstruct progress so recovery and status queries have an owner.
